facts: President Trump, speaking at the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas, pledged a $5,000 "Trump dividend" payment to every adult American citizen if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the November midterms.
Trump did not specify a funding source for the payments; using Census population data, the total cost of a $5,000 payment to all adult citizens would exceed $1 trillion.

Trump acknowledged Republicans "might not win" the midterms and delivered a speech lasting one hour and 44 minutes, longer than scheduled, covering tariffs, Iran's nuclear program, and proposed voter ID/registration legislation.
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) made a surprise 64-second video appearance at the convention to introduce Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.).

The convention's second night was scheduled to include a tribute to Charlie Kirk marking one year since his assassination at Utah Valley University, an observance of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, and remarks from Vice President Vance, Karoline Leavitt, Donald Trump Jr., and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Federal law prohibits paying or being paid to influence voting.
Public polls cited by NPR suggest Republicans may lose control of both the House and the Senate in the upcoming November midterms.
ladder.analysis: This was the first Republican midterm convention ever held, an event organized at Trump's initiative to energize the party base amid polling that suggests the GOP could lose one or both chambers of Congress in November. Trump's headline pledge — a $5,000 per-adult payment contingent on a GOP sweep — was delivered without a funding mechanism and at a cost analysts calculate would exceed $1 trillion, raising basic feasibility questions distinct from the legal issue that federal law bars paying voters to influence elections. Fetterman's brief video appearance, notable because he is a Democrat, was used within the convention program to introduce a Republican senator, illustrating the cross-partisan optics organizers sought amid a broader agenda that also memorialized Charlie Kirk on the anniversary of his killing and marked the 9/11 anniversary.
ladder.steelman: Regardless of political alignment, the pledge's core facts — no disclosed funding source, a cost exceeding $1 trillion, and a legal prohibition on paying voters to influence elections — are matters of arithmetic and existing statute, not partisan interpretation.
ladder.implications: How the $5,000 dividend proposal — which lacks a disclosed funding source and would cost more than $1 trillion — squares with the legal prohibition on paying voters to influence elections remains an open question heading into November. The midterm cycle is already shaped by redistricting disputes, such as the one in Missouri, and uncertain polling over which party will control Congress.

stories.headline: Incumbent governors lose primaries; anti-incumbent anger crosses party lines

claims.text: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee lost the Democratic gubernatorial primary to Helena Foulkes.
Dan McKee was the first sitting U.S. governor to lose a primary since Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer lost to Kris Kobach in 2018.
Jeff Colyer lost to Kris Kobach in 2018.

Helena Foulkes had previously lost to Dan McKee by a few percentage points in the 2022 Democratic primary.

The primary campaign centered on McKee's handling of the Washington Bridge.
The Washington Bridge was closed over structural concerns in December 2023.
The Washington Bridge remains under reconstruction.

Reed's campaign reported about $3.4 million in receipts through Aug. 20 compared with roughly $25,000 for Burbridge.
Elaine Pelino and Aaron Guckian were candidates in the Republican gubernatorial primary.
The Republican gubernatorial primary between Elaine Pelino and Aaron Guckian remained too close to call as of early results.

Rhode Island's 2026 primary season saw two prominent Democratic incumbents denied renomination.
Politico described a pattern of anti-incumbent sentiment crossing party lines.
Redistricting changes in some states compounded the anti-incumbent pattern.
A sitting governor and a sitting big-city mayor in Rhode Island were both denied renomination by their own party in the same election cycle.
Longtime U.S. senator Jack Reed fended off progressive primary challengers to win renomination.
The governor's race was shaped by a bridge closure and infrastructure management.
The mayor's race was shaped by housing costs and a vetoed rent-cap measure.
Reed's campaign reported a significant fundraising advantage over his primary opponents.

facts: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee lost the Democratic gubernatorial primary to Helena Foulkes, making him the first sitting U.S. governor to lose a primary since Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer lost to Kris Kobach in 2018.
Foulkes, a former CVS Health executive and current Costco board member, had previously lost to McKee by a few percentage points in the 2022 Democratic primary; the 2026 race was a rematch.

The primary campaign centered on McKee's handling of the Washington Bridge, which was closed over structural concerns in December 2023 and remains under reconstruction, versus Foulkes' record at CVS during its handling of opioid prescriptions.
Providence Mayor Brett Smiley lost the Democratic primary to State Rep. David Morales, 27, a democratic socialist endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, by a 54%-46% margin.

Sen. Jack Reed, 76, won his Democratic primary for a sixth term, defeating progressive challengers Connor Burbridge and Luis Muñoz; Reed's campaign reported about $3.4 million in receipts through Aug. 20 compared with roughly $25,000 for Burbridge.
The Republican gubernatorial primary between Elaine Pelino and Aaron Guckian remained too close to call as of early results.
Foulkes advances to the November general election against the GOP primary winner and independent candidates Ken Block, Jasjit "Jay" Gotra and Christopher "CD" Reynolds.

Morales advances to face Republican nominee Dave Talan, 77, in the November mayoral election; Republicans hold no seats on the Providence City Council and Kamala Harris carried the city by 51 points in 2024.
ladder.analysis: Rhode Island's 2026 primary season saw two prominent Democratic incumbents denied renomination, fitting a broader national pattern described by Politico of anti-incumbent sentiment crossing party lines, compounded by redistricting changes in some states. In Rhode Island specifically, a sitting governor and a sitting big-city mayor were both denied renomination by their own party in the same election cycle, while a longtime U.S. senator fended off progressive primary challengers to win renomination. The governor's and mayor's races were shaped by distinct local controversies — a bridge closure and infrastructure management for McKee, housing costs and a vetoed rent-cap measure for Smiley — while Reed's campaign reported a significant fundraising advantage over his primary opponents.
ladder.steelman: Across these races, the common thread is that voters showed a willingness to remove or seriously challenge sitting officeholders this cycle, echoing Politico's observation that anti-incumbent anger has crossed party lines nationally this year.
ladder.implications: With Foulkes now favored in the general election in heavily Democratic Rhode Island, and Morales advancing to face Republican nominee Dave Talan in a city where Republicans hold no council seats and Harris carried by 51 points in 2024, and the GOP gubernatorial primary outcome still pending, attention will shift to whether the anti-incumbent trend seen here recurs in other states' remaining primaries and whether it affects general-election outcomes in November.

stories.headline: Missouri redistricting battle escalates as Supreme Court asked to intervene; lawmakers threaten justices

claims.text: Missouri's legislature enacted a new congressional map (HB 1) in 2025.
The map was enacted at President Trump's urging.
The map was intended to give Republicans seven of the state's eight U.S. House seats.
The map reconfigured Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City-based 5th District.
The map was used in the state's August 2026 primary.
Opponents, organized as People Not Politicians and led by Richard von Glahn, submitted a referendum petition with more than 300,000 signatures last year.
The petition sought to let voters decide on the new map in the November 2026 election.
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) rejected that referendum petition on Aug. 4, 2026.
Hoskins argued the Missouri Constitution does not allow referendums on congressional redistricting plans.
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Sept. 3 that the referendum petition was legal, sufficient and timely.
The Missouri Supreme Court held the 2025 map 'was never in effect' and cannot be used unless voters approve it in November 2026.
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied Missouri's request for review of that ruling in a one-line order on Tuesday.
Kavanaugh's order left the state court's block on the map in place.
Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a temporary restraining order in a separate federal case brought by GOP Rep. Robert Onder.
Clark's order required the state to use the 2025 map instead.
The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined to pause Clark's order.
People Not Politicians filed a new emergency application with the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday asking it to block Clark's order.
Kavanaugh directed Onder and Hoskins to respond by 10 a.m. Thursday.
The Missouri Supreme Court ordered Hoskins to explain by Thursday why he should not be held in contempt for a Sept. 8 email instructing election officials to use the 2025 map.
A federal judge declined late Wednesday to halt that contempt hearing.
This dispute is part of a broader, unusual mid-decade redistricting push by Republicans nationally.
The redistricting push is encouraged by President Trump.
The push aims to redraw congressional maps ahead of the 2026 midterms rather than waiting for the next census cycle.
In Missouri, the fight centers on competing legal authorities: the Missouri Supreme Court says state constitutional referendum rights block the new map from taking effect until voters weigh in.
A federal judge issued a competing order requiring use of the 2025 map.
Hoskins has separately argued that the U.S. Constitution's Elections Clause gives the legislature control over federal election mechanics, superseding the referendum process.

The result has been a 24-hour cascade through four different courts — state supreme court, U.S. Supreme Court, federal district court, and the 8th Circuit — producing directly conflicting orders about which map applies.
The state's Secretary of State is caught between complying with a state court ruling and a federal injunction.
The Secretary of State faces a separate contempt threat for allegedly disobeying the state court.

The Supreme Court's response to Thursday's filing, combined with the outcome of the Missouri Supreme Court's contempt proceeding against Hoskins, will determine which congressional map — the 2022 or 2025 version — governs Missouri's November 2026 elections.
The outcome has implications for the balance of Missouri's U.S. House delegation.

Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City-based 5th District; that map was used in the state's August 2026 primary.

Opponents, organized as People Not Politicians and led by Richard von Glahn, submitted a referendum petition with more than 300,000 signatures last year seeking to let voters decide on the new map in the November 2026 election.
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) rejected that referendum petition on Aug. 4, 2026, arguing the Missouri Constitution does not allow referendums on congressional redistricting plans.

The Missouri Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Sept. 3 that the referendum petition was legal, sufficient and timely, holding the 2025 map 'was never in effect' and cannot be used unless voters approve it in November 2026.
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied Missouri's request for review of that ruling in a one-line order on Tuesday, leaving the state court's block on the map in place.

Minutes later, Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a temporary restraining order in a separate federal case brought by GOP Rep. Robert Onder, requiring the state to use the 2025 map instead; the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined to pause Clark's order.

People Not Politicians filed a new emergency application with the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday asking it to block Clark's order; Kavanaugh directed Onder and Hoskins to respond by 10 a.m. Thursday.

In a separate proceeding, the Missouri Supreme Court ordered Hoskins to explain by Thursday why he should not be held in contempt for a Sept. 8 email instructing election officials to use the 2025 map; a federal judge declined late Wednesday to halt that contempt hearing.

In Missouri, the fight centers on competing legal authorities: the Missouri Supreme Court says state constitutional referendum rights block the new map from taking effect until voters weigh in, while a federal judge issued a competing order requiring use of the 2025 map, and Hoskins has separately argued that the U.S. Constitution's Elections Clause gives the legislature control over federal election mechanics, superseding the referendum process. The result has been a 24-hour cascade through four different courts — state supreme court, U.S. Supreme Court, federal district court, and the 8th Circuit — producing directly conflicting orders about which map applies, with the state's Secretary of State caught between complying with a state court ruling and a federal injunction, and facing a separate contempt threat for allegedly disobeying the state court.
ladder.steelman: Beneath the partisan stakes, this dispute reflects a broader tension between state constitutional referendum authority and competing federal court orders, playing out under extreme time pressure that itself risks undermining confidence in the eventual outcome regardless of which map prevails.
ladder.implications: The Supreme Court's response to Thursday's filing, combined with the outcome of the Missouri Supreme Court's contempt proceeding against Hoskins, will determine which congressional map — the 2022 or 2025 version — governs Missouri's November 2026 elections, with implications for the balance of Missouri's U.S. House delegation.

stories.headline: Houthis seize port, US strikes five Iranian tankers, oil tops $100 as Middle East crisis deepens
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The United States destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran's Kharg Island on Tuesday, Central Command announced, as oil prices surged past $100 a barrel amid escalating conflict across the Middle East. The strikes bring to eight the number of Iranian crude tankers the US military has hit since Saturday in retaliation for Iranian attacks on US forces. On Monday, Iran retaliated by targeting US troops stationed at an air base in Jordan, using cluster munition ballistic missiles, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).

In Yemen, Houthi forces are testing the limits of Saudi restraint with intensified missile and drone attacks on civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, injuring dozens of civilians and causing fires and temporary disruption at energy facilities, Al Jazeera reported. The Houthis also continue to threaten maritime traffic in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical shipping lane. The attacks come as fighting intensifies along Yemen's western coast, where the Houthis are seeking to consolidate military positions overlooking the Red Sea.

The Houthi campaign presents Saudi Arabia with a difficult strategic equation, according to analysts cited by Al Jazeera. Riyadh has spent years trying to exit direct military involvement in Yemen and pursue a diplomatic settlement, but repeated attacks on Saudi territory and energy infrastructure are testing its restraint. Saudi Arabia has strengthened its air and missile defenses since the war's early years, but the Houthi arsenal now includes ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and increasingly sophisticated drones. Even when most incoming weapons are intercepted, relatively inexpensive systems can impose disproportionate defensive costs and create uncertainty around airports, industrial facilities, border communities and energy infrastructure, the report said.

On the economic front, the turmoil has pushed diesel prices in the US state of Idaho to nearly $6 a gallon, with AAA Idaho citing the escalating conflict between the United States and Iran and fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia over the Bab al-Mandeb shipping lane as the main drivers. "As long as those areas are supply chain chokepoints, crude oil prices will be under tremendous pressure," AAA Idaho public affairs director Matthew Conde said. The average price for regular unleaded in Idaho reached $4.76 a gallon, up 14 cents in a week. Nestle's CEO said the Middle East conflict is driving inflation and higher supplier costs, Reuters reported.

Iran has launched a concerted effort to more aggressively target US naval forces in recent days, likely seeking to degrade the United States' ability to enforce a naval blockade on Iranian ports, according to ISW analysis. Since September 4, Iran has fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier, Navy destroyers and at least one Marine vessel, with US officials describing some attacks as "close calls." US officials warned that Iran may be using "more sophisticated weapons," possibly the solid-fueled Qassem Basir medium-range ballistic missile with a maneuverable reentry vehicle, which can help evade air defenses. US officials also raised concerns that Russian or Chinese targeting assistance—including intelligence and satellite imagery—may have enabled Iran's recent attacks.

Iran appears to be targeting stationary commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman to deter further US strikes on Iranian oil tankers, ISW reported. The IRGC Navy issued an evacuation warning to tanker crews near Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports hosting US forces and threatened to attack crews "at anchor or at the ports." Iran is also framing its retaliation against vessels that do not comply with Iranian policies in the Strait of Hormuz as enforcement of its own "sanctions regime" to legitimize illegal activities against commercial shipping, ISW noted.

stories.headline: Russian jet-powered drones escalate Ukraine war, delay Zelensky flight
body: Russia fired its new jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating the use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to intercept. The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph — significantly faster than older models and beyond the top speed of Ukraine's interceptors. Ukrainian military intelligence says some of the turbojet engines powering the drones are sourced from China. The growing use of jet-propelled drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding 'horror' over Kyiv's skies.

Ukraine's military reported that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models. 'The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them,' said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London. The speed has prompted a new arms race: on 10 August, Ukraine’s deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles 'capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed'.

On Wednesday, a Russian drone incursion delayed Zelensky's flight from Chisinau, Moldova, where he was preparing to travel to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald V. Moldovan government spokesman Dumitru Ciorici told the BBC that Moldova closed its airspace after noticing a Russian drone had entered from Ukraine. Zelensky’s plane was left on the runway for about an hour before takeoff was authorised once the drone had come down and exploded some 160 km from the airport. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre initially said the flight was 'almost hit' by a drone, but a Ukraine source told AFP the risk had been 'exaggerated'. The Kremlin said there had been no threat to the jet.

The escalation comes as NATO 'military aviation' assets were deployed in Polish airspace overnight in response to Russian jet-powered drone attacks on targets in western Ukraine. Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command said the operations were preventive and aimed at ensuring the safety of Polish airspace. Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 149 drones into the country overnight, around half of which were jet-powered, along with decoy drones. Ukrainian defenses downed 128 drones, with impacts reported across 13 locations. In Kyiv, a drone hit a gas station, injuring three people; in Sumy, two people were killed and 23 injured in a strike on a shopping mall. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it also targeted two dry cargo ships heading to Odesa and claimed to have downed 448 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions.

Earlier this year Ukraine was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky, but the newer models have reduced effectiveness. Ukraine's Air Force data showed a drop in interceptions of ballistic missiles up to the end of July, and in August Kyiv mostly stopped publishing interception figures. Four Ukrainian companies have reportedly started testing missiles capable of shooting down the new Geran models, and the new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has tasked them with producing 'thousands of units' as quickly as possible. Meanwhile, satellite images appear to show Russia building a new drone launch base at Tsymbulova in the Oryol region, around 109 miles from the Ukrainian border, which has become a key centre for drone attacks since becoming operational.

The proliferation of jet-powered drones comes as BBC Verify found Russia is now striking Ukraine with complex attacks involving hundreds of drones and missiles about once a week. Analysts say the increase is driven by Moscow's shift to combining a greater variety of munitions with expensive ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to intercept. 'Long-range one-way attack drones are basically a poor man's cruise missile,' said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, noting that the line between drones and cruise missiles has become 'blurred'. However, Conflict Armament Research emphasised that jet-drones have shorter range, smaller warheads, and are more susceptible to jamming than cruise missiles. Ukraine has also struck back: its Special Operations Forces announced a 'record hit' on a Russian gas processing plant in the Yamalo-Nenets district, more than 3,000 km into Russia.

stories.headline: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia's Arctic gas heartland; Russian attacks kill 7 in Ukraine
body: Ukrainian drones struck deep into Russia's Arctic north on Wednesday, sparking a fire at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy, a city in the heart of Russia's most important natural-gas producing region, according to Russian officials and news agencies. Regional Governor Dmitry Artyukhov said Russian air defenses repelled the attack but falling drone debris caused a fire at an industrial site, without identifying the facility. He reported no casualties. Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SOF) confirmed the strike, calling it the deepest of the war at more than 3,000 kilometers (1,860 miles) from the border, and said it successfully hit two gas plants: Novy Urengoy and Purovsky in the Yamal-Nenets region.

Artem Zhoga, the Kremlin's envoy to the Urals, said it was the first strike ever to hit the Arctic part of the region. The Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug produces about 80% of Russia's natural gas, according to Interfax data. Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point appeared to claim involvement, posting online: 'Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target.' The attack was part of a broader Ukrainian drone assault that also targeted the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, where Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a naval base, oil terminal, military port facilities, and warships were struck. Russian authorities said four people, including a child, were killed and 29 wounded in Novorossiysk.

Russia retaliated with its own long-range attacks across Ukraine. In Mykolaiv, southern Ukraine, a Russian strike killed four people and wounded at least 19, according to acting Governor Heorhii Reshetilov. A drone attack on a shopping center in the northeastern city of Sumy killed three people and wounded at least 14, including three children, said local officials. The Russian Defence Ministry confirmed the Mykolaiv strike but said it targeted a drone warehouse, and also claimed hits on the port of Chornomorsk and two vessels near Odesa. Additionally, Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two civilians and wounding three, while a separate attack on Kyiv killed one and wounded 14, according to Reuters.

The escalation came as U.S. President Donald Trump said he spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested both sides may be prepared to negotiate. 'We had a great conversation. He is wanting to make a deal,' Trump told reporters on Wednesday, adding that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy might also be willing. Trump pointed to personal animosity between the two leaders, calling them 'two people that hate each other.' His comments followed a weekend diplomatic push by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Moscow and Kyiv but achieved no breakthrough. Russia resumed major missile and drone attacks on Kyiv shortly after the American delegation left, killing five on Tuesday.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that the simultaneous diplomacy and military escalation reflects a dilemma for Western governments: 'You have to talk, you have to explain' to prevent misunderstandings, but Russian officials can interpret outreach as 'Western weakness.' The source said Putin's emphasis on Russian military progress in Ukraine appeared aimed at projecting strength to Washington. The United Nations reported that Russian attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and over 2,600 wounded. More than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and over 51,000 wounded since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022. Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.

Ukraine's SOF described the Yamal strike as a historic first, saying the targeted area had been considered a 'safe rear zone' for Russia. The facilities process millions of tonnes of condensate per year from gas fields in the region, which Gazprom once exported to Western Europe until relations broke down after the war began. The region's gas resources are estimated at 26.5 trillion cubic metres, enough to cover global demand for more than six years. The attack underscores Ukraine's escalating long-range drone campaign, which Zelenskyy has said will make Russian airspace 'completely unsafe' for the duration of the war.

stories.headline: IAEA Board Refers Iran to UN Security Council for Nuclear Non-Compliance in Historic Vote
body: The Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) on Wednesday approved a resolution accusing Iran of failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations and referring the matter to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). The vote, the first of its kind in 20 years, saw at least 23 of the board's 35 member countries in favor; Russia, China and Niger opposed the measure. The resolution was sponsored by the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany.

The text expresses 'grave concern' over Iran's 'continued non-compliance' with its commitments under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), which forbids Iran from producing nuclear weapons and requires IAEA safeguards verification. The IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities—including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan—since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against Iran in June 2025. The agency estimates Iran holds about 400 kilograms (882 pounds) of highly enriched uranium, potentially enough to manufacture 10 nuclear weapons if enriched further. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the board on Monday that the lack of information and inability to conduct verification at these facilities is 'a matter of serious proliferation concern.'

Iran condemned the resolution as politically motivated and baseless. 'This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis,' said Reza Najafi, Iran's representative to the UN in Vienna. He argued that Iran has been unable to provide inspectors safe access due to ongoing military operations and persistent threats. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi accused the sponsors of a pretext: 'They attack Iran's safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution.' Iran's UN mission said the situation was caused by 'the criminal acts of aggression by the U.S. and Israeli regime.'

The diplomatic escalation comes more than six months into the US-Israeli war against Iran, amid heightened tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, where the US and Iran have traded attacks on vessels. The IAEA's referral to the UNSC is unlikely to result in further action, as Russia and China—both veto-holding permanent members—are expected to block any Western-backed measures. Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group called the resolution 'an exercise in futility.' The EU, in a statement, accused Iran of suspending cooperation and urged it to provide updated declarations and allow inspections to resume.

On the same day as the vote, US President Donald Trump renewed threats to target Iran's 'Pickaxe Mountain' underground complexes near the damaged Natanz facility, claiming the US had observed 'a little activity' there. Trump reiterated his assertion that Iran seeks a nuclear weapon, despite the IAEA having found no proof of a systematic effort to build one. Grossi told CNN, 'We did not have any proof of a systematic effort to move into a nuclear weapon.' The US launched its current military campaign saying Iran was on the verge of making a bomb—a claim not backed by the IAEA or US intelligence.

The IAEA board's previous criticism of Iran dates to the early 2000s, leading to UNSC sanctions in 2006. Iran remained in compliance with the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) until the US withdrew in 2018 and reimposed sanctions, prompting Tehran to intensify its nuclear program. In June 2025, the board declared Iran non-compliant shortly before the US-Israeli attacks. Tehran insists on its right to pursue civilian nuclear technology under the NPT and says it will cooperate with the IAEA only 'to the extent that circumstances and safety permit.'

stories.headline: Five dead, 86 missing after ferry fire off Philippines
body: At least five people have died and 86 remain missing after a fire broke out on a passenger ferry off the coast of the Philippine island of Palawan on Wednesday evening, the country's coastguard said. The MV June Aster was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members from Manila to the tourist destination of Coron when the blaze was reported at 18:45 local time (10:45 GMT), about 1.2 nautical miles (2.2 km) from Coron's Marcilla village. Forty-three people have been rescued, including two Chilean nationals.

Survivor Roland Lerma, a construction worker from Leyte province, told the BBC that as the fire spread he slipped and was trampled by other passengers before he crawled, found his footing, and leapt into the sea. 'When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions … so that I could float,' he said. Lerma floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived. 'If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died last night,' he said. A first responder described the scene as 'really heartbreaking'.

The coastguard said preliminary interviews with survivors suggest the fire started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion. The ship was carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods. The blaze was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday, and thick smoke, strong currents, extreme heat and the risk of explosions hampered search and rescue efforts. Drone footage released by the coastguard showed smoke still rising from the blackened vessel. The coastguard said it was using drift-modelling tools to identify areas where survivors might have been carried by currents, and air assets were on standby.

Families of the missing expressed anguish. Anelyn Magbanua, whose husband Marlon was on the ferry returning to Coron after visiting their children in Manila, told the BBC she had heard no news. 'I have been crying and praying since last night,' she said. Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy were also among the missing, family member Rai Garcia told the BBC. Garcia and his family made a poster appealing for information. Others posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for news of loved ones.
Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the ferry, expressed 'profound sadness' and said it was cooperating fully with authorities. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands where inter-island ferries are a cheap and vital mode of transport. Past disasters have been linked to overcrowding, rough weather, poor maintenance and lax enforcement of safety rules. In 2023, a fire on the MV Lady Mary Joy 3 killed 31 people off the country's south-western tip. With 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst in the Philippines in recent years.

stories.headline: Wholesale prices rose 0.4% in August, as expected, but energy costs keep inflation pressures alive
body: Wholesale prices in the U.S. rose 0.4% in August, in line with forecasts, according to a Labor Department report Thursday that could play a key role in the Federal Reserve's upcoming interest-rate decision. The producer price index, a measure of final-demand costs for goods and services, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, matching the Dow Jones consensus. On an annual basis, PPI stood at 5.4% — still well above the Fed's 2% inflation target and 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.

The report also included revisions and mixed underlying details. July's PPI was revised up to a 0.1% gain from the original estimate of no change. Excluding food and energy, core PPI accelerated by 0.2%, below the 0.3% forecast, while core less trade services — another volatile category — rose 0.3% for the month.

Energy prices and goods costs were responsible for most of the increase. Final-demand energy prices jumped 4.2%, pushed largely by soaring diesel, which surged 24.1%. Goods prices broadly advanced 1.1%. Services prices rose just 0.1%, with a 2.3% increase in transportation and warehousing accounting for much of that move. Portfolio management costs, a closely watched metric in the PPI calculations, fell 1.6% for the month but were still up 18.8% from a year ago.

The release coincided with U.S. crude oil prices topping $100 a barrel, and market reaction was negative: stock futures turned down and Treasury yields moved sharply higher. Analysts noted the wholesale inflation data was flogged by higher gasoline prices and marked the first of two inflation reports that will help dictate whether the Fed raises interest rates next week.

stories.headline: Fed Expected to Hold Rates Steady Through 2026, but Rising Number of Analysts See at Least One Hike
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the remainder of 2026, according to a Reuters poll, though a growing number of analysts now anticipate at least one rate hike before year-end. The central bank’s next policy decision is due at the Sept. 15-16 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, where investors are pricing in a 60% probability of a quarter-percentage-point increase, based on CME Group’s FedWatch tool. The meeting comes as inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2% target, with the August Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index reports due this week expected to show continued price pressures.

Economists surveyed by The Real Economy Blog forecast a 0.4% monthly increase in both headline CPI and PPI, with core CPI rising 0.2% and core PPI up 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, headline CPI is expected at 3.4% and core CPI at 2.5%; headline PPI is seen at 5.2% and core PPI at 4.6%. The blog’s author, Joe Brusuelas, noted that the risk is for CPI to arrive at a 0.5% monthly pace, and that rising oil prices—up 1.3% in August and more than 23% from a year ago—are a key factor driving inflation. The war with Iran, now in its seventh month, has kept crude above $90 per barrel, while tariffs and the build-out of artificial intelligence data centers are also contributing to persistent price increases.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has curtailed the use of forward guidance, leaving markets uncertain about the central bank’s next move. Marketplace reported that Warsh has kept his cards close to his chest ahead of the meeting, though he may begin laying out a better framework for decision-making. Randy Kroszner, an economist at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business, described the process as a “teething” period, adding that Warsh is learning what pieces the market needs to feel comfortable with his approach. The Fed has three tools to combat inflation—the balance sheet, communications, and the federal funds rate—but with balance sheet contraction off the table and communications confused, analysts say the federal funds rate will have to change if the FOMC intends to move inflation back to target.

President Donald Trump and senior administration officials have publicly urged the Fed to lower rates, arguing the U.S. should have the lowest interest rates to avoid an economic disadvantage. In a Sept. 4 post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart — BE PATRIOTS for a change.” However, many economists warn that cutting rates prematurely would be counterproductive. Mark Higgins, senior vice president at Index Fund Advisors, said history shows the most reliable way to restore price stability is to maintain sufficiently restrictive policy until inflation is decisively tamed, and that a rate hike would send a clear message in the best interest of the American people. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s, argued that a Fed cut would signal a loss of independence from the president, leading to expectations of even higher inflation and causing long-term rates to rise substantially further.

For consumers, a rate hike would increase borrowing costs on car loans, credit card debt, and mortgages. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield briefly topped 4.8% on Tuesday, pushing the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate to 6.89%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Zandi warned that fixed mortgage rates, which have risen from below 6% before the war with Iran, could surge above 7% if the Fed cuts rates, and that borrowing costs for businesses and commercial property owners would also rise. Mark Hamrick, an economic analyst and founder of The Hamrick Brief, noted that persistently high prices have weighed especially heavily on middle- and lower-income households, many of which are struggling to afford basic necessities. He emphasized that preserving the Fed’s credibility is paramount, as a loss of faith in the central bank’s ability to restore price stability could make inflation more difficult to control.

The upcoming CPI and PPI data will be critical in determining the Fed’s next move. The Real Economy Blog stated that for the Fed not to hike, it would need to see a top-line monthly CPI increase of 0.25% or less. With inflation having remained above target for more than five years, and what were once thought to be temporary factors now appearing persistent, the pressure on the Fed to act is mounting. The September meeting also comes just weeks before the November midterm elections, as polls show voters broadly dissatisfied with high prices and elevated borrowing costs. The Economist has argued that Warsh should raise rates, while Bloomberg noted that the chairman’s honeymoon period is ending as the central bank faces three choices on how to proceed.

stories.headline: Seahawks rally past Patriots 13-10 in NFL opener; Darnold injured, Maye throws three fourth-quarter interceptions
body: The defending champion Seattle Seahawks overcame a 10-0 deficit and the loss of starting quarterback Sam Darnold to a hip injury on their opening drive to defeat the New England Patriots 13-10 in the 2026 NFL season opener Wednesday night at Lumen Field. Backup quarterback Drew Lock led the comeback, while Patriots quarterback Drake Maye threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter, including a game-sealing pick in the end zone with 21 seconds remaining.

Darnold was injured on Seattle's first possession and did not return. Head coach Mike Macdonald said initial tests indicated Darnold had not fractured his hip. Lock, who took over and struggled early, completed the key play of the game on a fourth-and-1 from the Patriots' 45-yard line with under 12 minutes to play. He found wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a play-action pass, and Smith-Njigba — last season's offensive player of the year — raced 45 yards for a touchdown that tied the game at 10. Lock admitted after the game that he had never practiced that specific play.

The Patriots had taken a 10-0 lead in the second quarter on a touchdown catch by rookie tight end Eli Raridon, the first touchdown of the NFL season. New England's defense limited Seattle to three points through three quarters, and Maye completed 17 of 22 passes for a touchdown and no interceptions in the first three periods. But the game unraveled in the fourth quarter. Seahawks cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett intercepted a Maye pass deflected by rookie Rodney Thomas to set up Lock's touchdown pass. After Julian Love picked off Maye on the next possession, kicker Jason Myers hit a 26-yard field goal to give Seattle a 13-10 lead.

Maye's third interception came with the Patriots driving for a potential game-tying or winning score. From well within field-goal range with 21 seconds left, Maye threw a pass toward Mack Hollins that was intercepted in the end zone by Seahawks defensive back Josh Jobe. Maye finished 23 of 33 for 178 yards, one touchdown and three interceptions. According to OptaSTATS, the Patriots became the first NFL team in the last 30 years to record at least three interceptions, three sacks, three penalties and zero points in a single quarter. Maye called his final interception "unacceptable," adding, "We could have sent it to overtime at the worst, and the only thing I could do was turn the ball over." Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said, "You can't throw three interceptions. Drake knows that."

The Patriots also lost star wide receiver A.J. Brown to an ankle injury during the game. New England's rushing attack was ineffective, and the team struggled to handle Seattle's blitzes. The Seahawks' defense, known as 'the Dark Side' during their Super Bowl run, recorded three sacks in the fourth quarter after allowing none in the first three. Seattle extended its winning streak to 11 games. Week 1 continues with the NFL's first regular-season game in Australia, as the Los Angeles Rams face the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne on Thursday. The Patriots next host the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sept. 20, while the Seahawks travel to face the Arizona Cardinals on the same date.

stories.headline: Apple's foldable iPhone Duo becomes official; AirPods 5 and Watch Series 12 also debut
body: Apple today unveiled a slate of new hardware at its fall event, including the long-rumored iPhone Duo foldable, which starts at $1,999 and features a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR foldable display when opened and a 5.4-inch outer screen with an asymmetric design. The company also introduced the $129 AirPods 5 with improved active noise cancellation and transparency mode, the Watch Series 12 starting at $399, and the Ultra 4 starting at $799, both with a new Health Sensing System and S11 chip. Additionally, Apple announced the iPhone 18 Pro, featuring a variable aperture camera and the first 2 nm A20 Pro chip. Preorders are open for the AirPods 5, Watch Series 12, and Ultra 4, with shipments beginning September 18.

The iPhone Duo, revealed during Apple's classic "One more thing" segment, adopts a passport-like shape when closed and a 1:1.4 aspect ratio both open and closed. Apple criticized earlier foldables with square aspect ratios, saying they are bad for single apps and video. The Duo's display uses multiple layers of flexible glass, a titanium base, and a custom polymer top layer with nano-texture finish to reduce the visible crease—a claim Apple says the device will not develop a crease over time. The outer screen has pointy corners on the hinge side and rounded corners on the opposite side, which Apple says "invites you to open" the phone. At $1,999, the Duo is priced similarly to foldables from Google and Samsung.

The AirPods 5, priced at $129 for the base model and $149 with a wireless charging case and on-stem volume control, offer active noise cancellation that Apple says removes up to 50 percent more noise than the AirPods 4, thanks to a new multiport acoustic architecture and improved computational audio. An enhanced transparency mode lets users hear nearby sounds more naturally, and adaptive audio automatically shifts between cancellation and transparency based on background noise, according to Dave Pakula, VP of hardware engineering at Apple. Preorders are open now.

The Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 feature a new Health Sensing System with redesigned photodiodes in a ring and larger, more power-efficient green LEDs that measure heart rate every five seconds. The S11 chip enables heart rate variability (HRV) measurements up to 24 times more frequently than previous models, and the watches deliver the "most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable" based on a study of over 1,000 participants. New features include a readiness score from 0 to 10 that analyzes activity, training load, vitals, and sleep, and a Health Age score in the iOS Health app later this year. Apple Intelligence features include Shazam detection, Live Rewind (showing the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as text), and Siri Recap for high-level summaries. Aluminum versions of the Watch Series 12 are 60 percent tougher than prior models, and optional ceramic and titanium finishes are available.

The iPhone 18 Pro, also announced, includes a variable aperture mechanical iris in the main camera allowing f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4 settings, with manual controls for shutter speed, white balance, and focusing now built into the native camera app. The Verge noted that the f/1.48 maximum aperture is the more significant improvement, improving low-light performance and bokeh. The A20 Pro chip, the first 2 nm processor for iPhone, has a 6-core CPU with two super-cores up to 20 percent faster and a 7-core GPU with up to 40 percent improved performance. Apple also highlighted Apple Intelligence features, including the previously announced LLM-driven Siri AI arriving in October, and argued the iPhone provides ideal context for AI features while maintaining privacy.

stories.headline: Mathematicians challenge OpenAI's Navier-Stokes solution, demand proof of data use
body: Two mathematicians have publicly accused OpenAI of unethical behavior and a lack of transparency over how the company's AI models achieved recent breakthroughs, including a solution to the legendary Navier-Stokes problem. Andreas Thom, a mathematician at the University of Leipzig, posted on Mastodon that OpenAI's responses to his questions about whether his interactions with ChatGPT contributed to a result on non-sofic groups were 'dishonest.' His challenge follows Tristan Buckmaster, a New York University professor, who earlier questioned whether OpenAI used his Codex sessions to help solve Navier-Stokes.

In a blog post last month, OpenAI announced that its model solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a millennium prize question about fluid movement, in 88 hours using a swarm of 10,000 AI agents. The company acknowledged its non-sofic groups result built heavily on previous work by Thom and fellow mathematician Gábor Kun, later amending its writeup after criticism. But Thom said he was struck by 'OpenAI's detailed command of our techniques,' which he called neither obvious nor promising. He asked researchers Sébastien Bubeck and Mark Sellke whether his ChatGPT conversations were part of training data. Thom said Sellke's answer only addressed direct access, not indirect influence through de-identified data. 'I take this as dishonesty to say the least,' Thom wrote.

OpenAI has flatly denied using any specific user data. In its Navier-Stokes announcement, the company stated: 'We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem.' However, it added: 'While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.' Thom said that de-identification 'does not remove the intellectual content of a mathematical idea.' Buckmaster similarly reported that after contacting OpenAI about its awareness of his progress, an OpenAI researcher asked him 'Why would you ruin your career?' and later said 'If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.' Buckmaster said OpenAI urged him to drop coauthor Levent Alpöge, though Bubeck disputed that.

The controversy has shocked mathematicians, who see OpenAI's conduct as a violation of longstanding academic norms of openness and trust. OpenAI said it began working on Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors on Twitter that other researchers were making progress. The company spent millions on the effort but said it has no plan to claim the $1 million bounty. Researchers told The Verge they fear such behavior could push mathematics toward secrecy, knowing that even rumors of progress could trigger a race with a well-resourced tech giant. 'Mathematics depends heavily on an informal norm of trust,' said Matthew Ballard, a University of South Carolina professor. 'Researchers routinely share incomplete ideas... it is done with the expectation that it will not turn into a competition.'

Thom said that only OpenAI 'has the relevant data' to prove whether user data influenced its results, and he called on the company to disclose datasets and clarify its data-use policies. 'It would be ethically indefensible,' he said, if nonpublic research from users helped improve models that OpenAI then used to race those same users to publication without consent, disclosure, or credit. OpenAI did not immediately respond to The Verge's request for comment on the latest allegations.

The ongoing dispute underscores a broader unease in the mathematical community, even as OpenAI's achievement in solving the Navier-Stokes problem – if verified – would be an extraordinary milestone. The company's reluctance to rule out indirect data use, combined with its aggressive pursuit of a result after hearing rumors, has left many mathematicians wary. As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, put it, OpenAI has engaged in the 'kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.'
